plan: Second-price sealed-bid auction with two opponents. Dominant strategy is to bid true value because the price paid equals the second-highest bid; shading risks losing profitable wins without reducing payment when winning. No prior history to exploit and only one round, so no strategic signaling or adaptation. My value is $22, so I set my maximum acceptable price at 22 to win whenever the second-highest bid is below 22 and otherwise lose, maximizing expected profit.

[ This is a second-price (Vickrey) auction with independent private values uniformly drawn each round. In such auctions, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit regardless of others’ strategies. Overbidding risks negative payoff if a higher rival bid sets a price above my value; underbidding risks losing when I would have earned positive surplus. With value 34 and no useful history (single round), I bid exactly 34 to win whenever the second-highest bid is below 34 and pay that second-highest bid. Ties are random; exact truth-telling remains optimal. ]

[ In a second-price sealed-bid auction with independent private values, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: it maximizes expected profit and avoids winning at a price above your value. Underbidding risks losing profitable cases; overbidding risks winning when the second-highest bid exceeds your value. There’s only one round and no history to exploit, so I simply set my maximum acceptable price equal to my value. Therefore, I bid exactly 10.0. ]
